source.title: Evaluating Adversarial Robustness of Concept Representations in Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Aaron J. Li; Suraj Srinivas; Usha Bhalla; Himabindu Lakkaraju

record.file_problem: not stated; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports on the robustness of sparse-autoencoder (SAE) representations under input perturbations. It does not test whether neuron poles have one or more human-interpretable jobs, nor test the explanation-fidelity claims in V6 or V7. Its results concern a related but different construct, so they are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses interpretability and monosemanticity but measures robustness of SAE latents, not neuron-pole job counts or the predictive accuracy of explanations. The listed rows record its relevant SAE-robustness and semantic-preservation results; none measures a version as stated.
record.test_reason: The study measures how SAE latents on Gemma2 and Llama3 respond to one-token adversarial and synonym perturbations. It does not audit native neurons' jobs (V1–V4), build neuron attribution graphs (V5), or score neuron explanations against held-out firing (V6, V7). SAE latents are a different unit from the model's own neurons. The attacks are adversarial rather than natural-text prediction tests. So the results fall under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Authors conclude SAE concept representations are fragile to minimal input perturbations while the base LLM stays semantically stable, and may be ill-suited for monitoring without denoising. They add that this is not a verdict against SAEs and suggest the attacks could help filter non-robust interpretations.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses input-space adversarial and synonym perturbations to evaluate SAE representation robustness; it does not conduct a neuron-pole interpretability audit or test explanations on held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports differing attack behavior by semantic goal, activation level, model depth, dataset, model/SAE pair, and transfer between models. Targeted population attacks weaken with depth while untargeted population attacks become more effective.

fits_no_version.finding: One-token synonym swaps cut SAE top-k concept overlap with the original from 100% to about 66–73% across five model/SAE pairs. They never flip the individual status of selected latents.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE population-level concept representations shift substantially under non-adversarial one-token synonym changes.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear probes on base-LLM activations show FNR changes of 0–4.5 points after adversarial perturbation; the authors call these not significant.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial tokens that move SAE latents leave dataset-level concepts in base-LLM activations largely intact.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix I: untargeted attacks deactivate highly interpretable Neuronpedia SAE latents on their top-activating sentences. The edits insert unrelated tokens elsewhere in the sequence. Qualitative only, with no rates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interpretable SAE latents' firing can be suppressed by semantically irrelevant one-token edits, so their labels do not fully predict when they fire.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The paper notes compute constraints and that experiments and hyperparameter choices used a single 80GB A100 GPU. Probe test accuracy is stated as at least 90% on original x1 instances; Table 2 describes differences as not significant but gives no uncertainty values there. The study targets medium-sized models and states that results are not identical across LLM-SAE pairs.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable; the included rows are from Tables 2 and 3. Other adversarial-attack result grids and depth/transfer analyses are not included because they measure SAE attack efficacy, not any of the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit shares (one job, two jobs, not understood).
Neuron interpretability shares across other dense and MoE models and scales.
Reinterpretation of the InceptionV1 cat/car neuron and recursive generalization.
Whether architecture, regularization and tools drive the share of interpretable neurons.
Neuron-based attribution graphs without replacement models.
Whether neuron explanations from activating examples predict firing on other text.
Simulation-based automated scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: All rows concern SAE latents, not native neurons, so none link to a version. Main adversarial attack grids (Figs 2, 4–13), depth and transfer results are reasonably omitted since they likewise bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit shares for one job, two related jobs, and not-yet-understood poles.
Interpretability shares across models, architectures, and parameter scales.
Whether the InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron detects pose or exemplifies recursive generalization.
Whether architecture, regularization, and tools explain interpretability shares or produce the stated InceptionV1-sized-model estimates.
Whether neuron-based attribution graphs explain behavior without a replacement model and its reconstruction error.
Whether explanations based on activating examples predict firing on other activations.
Automated scores for neuron explanations simulated on new text.

rows.subject: Gemma2-2B (16k)
rows.operation_detail: Replace one token with a synonym; report constrained-synonym attack result.
rows.measure: Population concept-overlap result, as reported in Table 3; paper says synonym replacement reduces overlap by roughly 30%.
rows.note: The table reports the population value as 73.4; the text characterizes the overall result as roughly a 30% decrease in concept overlap.
rows.check: Baseline should be 100% (overlap of x1 with itself before perturbation), not 'not stated'. 73.4 is the post-synonym overlap, about a 27-point drop.

rows.locator: Table 2; Section 4.3, Decoupling SAE and LLM Robustness
rows.note: The paper says the differences are not significant and that dataset-level concepts remain largely preserved in LLM activations.
